To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the best interest of children is an argument for state involvement in the process of assessing parent potential only when the state itself has contributed to the creation of a family.

the state assesses the parent potential of persons who are not yet biological parents only when the state is involved in the creation of the family, and that the best interest of children is not used as an argument in such assessments.
in Sweden the best interest of children is used as an argument to assess the parent potentials of individuals in situations where there are no or limited biogenetic ties between parents and children.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the ways in which social policy and social work practices in Sweden are shaped by the concept of best interests of the child.
the question of how the state, through assessments of parent potential rather parental performance, aims at controlling and regulating parenthood in Sweden.
the ways in which social and cultural norms and ideals are translated into legal norms and ideals.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
state-authorized assessments are made only when the state contributes to the creation or the maintenance of the family, but not when it aims to prevent it.

the state’s interest in the best interest of children has been used to justify assessments of the parent potential of those persons who have been involved in the creation of families with no or only partial genetic links to their children, but not to justify assessments of those who are not involved in the creation process.
the best interest of a child is not an argument for assessments of parent potential in the cases of adoption and assisted reproduction in Sweden.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the argument of the best interest for the child is not used as a tool to protect children, but as a tool to regulate the creation of new families.
the state is more willing to assess the parent potentials of persons who are involved in the creation of families that are not biogenetically linked than those who are.
the best interest of children is not an argument for the state to assess parent potential.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the best interest of a child is not a sufficient argument for state-authorization of assessments of parent potential.
the best interest of a child is used to argue for state involvement in the creation of a family when the child has no biological connection to one or both of the parents.
the state has a strong interest in assessing parent potential in cases where it contributes to the formation of a family, but not in cases where it does not.
